cards.lead: At high latitudes during summer, biphasic sleep aligned to actual sunset/sunrise maintains circadian coherence better than blackout curtains.
cards.body_markdown: A forum member in Stockholm (59.3°N) describes a biphasic sleep protocol adapted to the actual light environment rather than using blackout curtains. Using blackout curtains to create artificial darkness during long summer nights creates a circadian mismatch: the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) receives a darkness signal while the sun is actually above the horizon. This is an artificial twilight that does not match geographic and seasonal reality. Instead, the protocol follows the actual light cycle: sleep at sunset (~21:00) when melatonin rises naturally, wake at sunrise (~03:41) for a 30-minute barefoot walk to the lake for cold immersion and head dunks, return home, open the window fully, and sleep again until ~08:00. Total sleep is ~10 hours across two periods. This allows catching both sunrise and sunset every day, using the open window for continued light input on skin and eyelids during the second sleep, while maintaining sufficient total sleep for glyphatic deuterium clearance and full recovery.
